source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Euclidean algorithm
statement: Repeated division with remainder computes gcd(a,b) and produces integers u,v with ua+vb=gcd(a,b).
conditions: a and b are integers, not both zero.
conclusion: The final nonzero remainder is the gcd and a Bezout identity is obtained.
typical_uses: Solve linear Diophantine equations and invert modulo m.
common_misuses: Stopping before the last nonzero remainder.
bridge_lemmas: gcd is unchanged by replacing (a,b) with (b,a mod b).
repair_templates: Record every remainder step and back-substitute.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Chinese remainder theorem
statement: For pairwise coprime moduli m_i, simultaneous congruences x=a_i modulo m_i have a unique solution modulo the product of the moduli.
conclusion: The residue ring modulo the product is isomorphic to the product of the residue rings.
typical_uses: Solve systems of congruences and factor computations modulo composite integers.
common_misuses: Applying uniqueness modulo the product when moduli are not coprime.
bridge_lemmas: Bezout inverses of each partial product.
repair_templates: Check pairwise gcds and construct idempotent coefficients.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Linear congruence solvability
statement: ax=b modulo m is solvable iff gcd(a,m) divides b; when solvable it has exactly gcd(a,m) incongruent solutions modulo m.
conclusion: Solvability and solution count are determined by gcd(a,m).
common_misuses: Cancelling a nonunit coefficient modulo m.
repair_templates: Divide by the gcd only after verifying divisibility of b.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Euler criterion
statement: For an odd prime p and a not divisible by p, a is a quadratic residue modulo p iff a^((p-1)/2) is congruent to 1 modulo p; otherwise it is congruent to -1.
conditions: p is an odd prime and p does not divide a.
conclusion: The Legendre symbol (a/p) equals a^((p-1)/2) modulo p.
common_misuses: Applying the criterion at p=2 or when p divides a.
bridge_lemmas: Fermat's little theorem and the cyclic structure of the multiplicative group.
repair_templates: Separate the cases p divides a, p=2, and odd prime p.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Quadratic reciprocity law
statement: For distinct odd primes p and q, (p/q)(q/p)=(-1)^(((p-1)/2)((q-1)/2)).
conditions: p and q are distinct odd primes.
conclusion: Legendre symbols can be interchanged with the stated sign correction.
typical_uses: Evaluate Legendre symbols and solve quadratic congruences.
common_misuses: Forgetting the supplementary signs for -1 and 2.
repair_templates: Reduce to odd prime factors and apply the sign formula carefully.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Character orthogonality
statement: Dirichlet characters modulo m satisfy sum over residues chi(n) conjugate(psi(n)) equal to phi(m) when chi=psi and zero otherwise.
conditions: chi and psi are Dirichlet characters modulo m.
conclusion: Characters form an orthogonal basis for functions on the unit group modulo m.
typical_uses: Extract coefficients in character expansions and prove L-function identities.
common_misuses: Summing over nonunits without extending characters by zero.
bridge_lemmas: Finite abelian group character sums vanish for nontrivial characters.
repair_templates: Specify the summation domain and character convention.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Mobius inversion
statement: If F(n)=sum_{d|n} f(d), then f(n)=sum_{d|n} mu(d)F(n/d), where mu is the Mobius function.
conditions: f and F are arithmetic functions related by divisor summation.
conclusion: Divisor convolution with the Mobius function inverts the divisor-sum operator.
common_misuses: Using additive rather than multiplicative divisor convolution.
bridge_lemmas: sum_{d|n} mu(d) equals 1 for n=1 and 0 otherwise.
repair_templates: Rewrite the relation as Dirichlet convolution before inverting.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Multiplicativity under Dirichlet convolution
statement: The Dirichlet convolution of multiplicative arithmetic functions is multiplicative; the identity is supported at 1.
conditions: f and g are multiplicative arithmetic functions.
typical_uses: Derive Euler products and factor divisor sums.
common_misuses: Using multiplicativity when m and n are not coprime.
bridge_lemmas: Divisors of coprime products split uniquely.
repair_templates: Insert the coprimality hypothesis before factoring the divisor sum.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Pell equation via units
statement: Solutions of x^2-Dy^2=1 correspond to norm-one units in Z[sqrt(D)]; powers of a fundamental unit generate all positive solutions under standard hypotheses.
conditions: D is a nonsquare positive integer and the quadratic order is fixed.
conclusion: The solution set has a multiplicative recurrence generated by a fundamental unit.
typical_uses: Construct infinite families of Diophantine solutions.
common_misuses: Assuming every D has an elementary fundamental solution without computation.
bridge_lemmas: Norm is multiplicative in the quadratic ring.
repair_templates: Identify the relevant order and verify norm one.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Hensel lifting criterion
statement: A simple root of a polynomial modulo p lifts uniquely to roots modulo every higher power p^k.
conditions: f(a) is congruent to 0 modulo p and f'(a) is not congruent to 0 modulo p.
conclusion: There is a unique compatible sequence of roots modulo p^k.
typical_uses: Solve polynomial congruences over p-adic integers.
common_misuses: Applying simple-root uniqueness when the derivative vanishes modulo p.
bridge_lemmas: Correct the lift one digit at a time using a linearized congruence.
repair_templates: Check the derivative condition at the initial root.
